title: IDL: improving a SolidWorks workflow
summary: At IDL Worldwide, our team brought drawing turnaround from roughly eight hours to roughly two. I extended the shared SolidWorks techniques through reusable store layouts, model organization, and personal refinement, reaching a reported 37-minute drawing time.
highlights: Team improvement: approximately 8 hours to 2 hours

hero.title: IDL: improving a SolidWorks workflow
hero.subtitle: From repeatedly modeling stores from scratch to building with reusable layouts and configurable components.
hero.summary: Store audits supplied measurements and mechanical drawings of ceilings, soffits, electrical points, existing fixtures, and install areas. We recreated stores in SolidWorks, then extracted installation drawings. Coworkers introduced blocks and common layout patterns. I contributed to those libraries, built reusable store configurations and an efficient SolidWorks model structure, and refined my own drawing practice.

overview.title: Store drawings for a national retail rollout
overview.description: At IDL Worldwide, I digitized more than 500 AT&T retail locations in SolidWorks to support Apple fixture installation. Survey notes and mechanical drawings informed layered 3D models of store architecture, electrical points, and fixtures. Installation drawing views were extracted from those models and passed to the installation team. Early drawings took roughly eight hours apiece.

media.title: Store drawings for the AT&T rollout

solution.title: Create reusable building blocks instead of redrawing every store
solution.description: The team used shared shortcuts and libraries to reduce drawing turnaround to roughly two hours. I developed additional reusable store layouts, configurable fixture assemblies, a more efficient model information structure, and increasingly precise personal techniques. My later individual turnaround reached a reported 37 minutes. These improvements were not separately timed.

steps.title: Read the store audit
steps.description: Use on-site measurements, notes and mechanical drawings covering soffits, ceilings, electrical, existing fixtures, and installation areas.

steps.title: Reuse common patterns
steps.description: Build from familiar store layout configurations. Coworkers introduced reusable blocks and common patterns; I expanded the libraries and created additional layouts.

steps.title: Adapt fixture assemblies
steps.description: Use configurable sub-assemblies for fixture variants instead of reproducing repeated geometry.

steps.title: Organize the SolidWorks model
steps.description: Structure architecture, electrical, and fixture placement information so the model can be assembled and modified quickly.

steps.title: Extract and review installation drawings
steps.description: Produce mechanical drawing views from the layered 3D model, request QC promptly, and pass drawings to the installation team.

impact.title: Drawing turnaround and delivery scope
impact.description: Initial and team-stage figures are approximate retrospective turnaround estimates, not a formal controlled timing study. The approximately two-hour result belongs to the team. The later 37-minute result is an individual report. The figures reflect combined improvements, not separately measured savings per technique or savings for every one of the 500+ locations. Financial savings, reduced stress, and worker autonomy were not measured.

conclusion.title: What this work contributes
conclusion.description: This work taught me to look for repeated patterns in a system and to build reusable structures around them. Team knowledge-sharing, new layouts, and clear model organization made repetitive production more efficient. It is design-engineering process improvement, not a claim of having formally measured UX outcomes.
